The math of their sides and angles is named from Greek words for this shape and “measure”

trap.title: Any shape or one kind?
trap.body: Some tossups want one specific kind: equilateral (all sides equal), isosceles (at least two equal sides), scalene (no equal sides), or right (one 90° angle). On those, plain “triangle” may earn only a prompt, so be ready to add the type. Other tossups want the Pythagorean theorem, which works only for right ones, or Pascal’s triangle, which is a pattern of numbers rather than a shape.
trap.fix: Listen to the giveaway. If it says “three-sided polygon” with clues true of every one (angles add up to 180°, area is one-half × base × height), say “triangle.” If it gives a defining detail like “all three sides equal” or “one 90-degree angle,” name that kind.
trap.line: Real answer line: triangles (accept specific kinds, such as equilateral triangles; prompt on polygons or shapes)

topics.name: Circles
topics.kicker: Every point the same distance from the center · C = πd and A = πr²
topics.dates: Studied in Book III of Euclid’s Elements, c. 300 BCE
topics.briefing: A circle is the set of all points in a flat plane that sit the same distance, called the radius, from one center point. A straight segment through the center from edge to edge is the diameter, twice as long as the radius, and the distance around, the circumference, is always about 3.14 times the diameter, a number called π. Wheels, gears, and pizzas use this shape, and its area is π times the radius squared.
topics.answerHtml: circles (prompt on disks, ellipses, or conic sections; do not accept “diameter” or “sphere”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1882, Ferdinand von Lindemann proved that it is impossible to use only a compass and straightedge to draw a square with exactly the same area as this shape. Among all closed curves with the same perimeter, this shape encloses the most area.
tossups.r: A chord through its center is called a diameter. For 10 points, name this shape whose area equals pi times its radius squared.

tossups.p: Frederick Soddy’s 1936 poem “The Kiss Precise” restates a rule, first found by René Descartes, about the sizes of four of these shapes that all touch one another. The curvature of one of these shapes equals 1 divided by its radius.
tossups.r: Its radius is the distance from its center to its edge. For 10 points, name this round shape whose circumference equals pi times its diameter.

tossups.p: An angle formed by two chords that meet on this shape is exactly half of the central angle that cuts off the same arc. In a quadrilateral whose four corners all lie on this shape, opposite angles add up to 180 degrees.
tossups.r: Every point on this shape is the same distance from its center. For 10 points, name this shape, whose radius is half its diameter.

tossups.p: Book III of Euclid’s _Elements_ is devoted to this shape. Thales [“THAY-leez”] is credited with proving that if a triangle has all three corners on this shape and one side passes through its center, the angle opposite that side is a right angle.
tossups.r: Its distance around is called its circumference. For 10 points, name this shape, whose diameter is twice its radius.

tossups.p: Apollonius of Perga posed the problem of drawing every one of these shapes that touches three given ones of them. He also showed that the points whose distances from two fixed points always have the same ratio, other than 1, form one of these shapes.
tossups.r: Its area equals pi times its radius squared. For 10 points, name this shape, which has a center, a radius, and a diameter.

tossups.p: Ptolemy’s theorem says that for a quadrilateral with its corners on this shape, the two diagonals multiply to the sum of the products of opposite sides. When two chords of this shape cross, the pieces of one chord multiply to the same number as the pieces of the other.
tossups.r: Its diameter is its longest chord. For 10 points, name this shape, which also has a radius and a circumference.

tossups.p: Archimedes showed that the area of this shape equals the area of a right triangle whose two legs are its radius and its circumference. Legend says that when Roman soldiers captured Syracuse, Archimedes was busy drawing these shapes in the sand and told a soldier not to disturb them.
tossups.r: Its circumference is a little more than three times its diameter. For 10 points, name this shape, whose area is pi times the radius squared.

tossups.p: The cosine and sine of an angle are the x- and y-coordinates of a point on the one of these shapes that has radius 1 and is centered at the origin. The graph of x squared plus y squared equals 25 is one of these shapes with a radius of 5.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this shape made of all the points at a fixed distance from a center.

tossups.p: This shape is the conic section formed when a plane slices a cone at a right angle to the cone’s axis. It is the special ellipse with an eccentricity of zero, because its two foci are at the same point.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this shape, in which every point is the same distance from the center.

tossups.p: One radian is the angle at the center of this shape that cuts off an arc exactly as long as its radius. The length of any arc of this shape equals its radius times the arc’s angle measured in radians.
tossups.r: A full turn around its center is 360 degrees. For 10 points, name this shape, whose distance around is called its circumference.

tossups.p: The ring-shaped region between two of these shapes that share a center is called an annulus. Two tangent segments drawn to one of these shapes from the same outside point have equal lengths, and each is perpendicular to the radius at the point where it touches.
tossups.r: A line that touches it at only one point is called a tangent. For 10 points, name this shape, whose circumference is pi times its diameter.

tossups.p: In Ptolemy’s model of the heavens, each planet moved along a small one of these shapes called an epicycle, whose center rode along a larger one. Johannes Kepler later showed that planets actually orbit in ellipses instead of these perfectly round paths.
tossups.r: It has infinitely many lines of symmetry. For 10 points, name this shape, whose area equals pi times its radius squared.

tossups.p: Every triangle has exactly one of these shapes passing through all three of its corners, centered at a point called the circumcenter. John Venn’s diagrams for comparing two or three sets are usually drawn as overlapping ones of these shapes.
tossups.r: A slice of it shaped like a piece of pizza is called a sector. For 10 points, name this round shape, whose diameter is twice its radius.

tossups.p: The third of Euclid’s five postulates says that one of these shapes can be drawn with any center and any radius. In classical Greek geometry, the tool that draws these shapes and an unmarked straightedge were the only tools allowed for constructions.
tossups.r: That tool is a compass. For 10 points, name this shape, whose radius runs from its center to its edge.

tossups.p: Hippocrates of Chios [“KY-oss”] found the exact areas of some crescent-shaped regions, called lunes, that are bounded by arcs of two of these shapes. Archimedes drew 96-sided polygons inside and outside one of these shapes to prove that its distance around is between 223 over 71 and 22 over 7 times its width.
tossups.r: The ratio of its circumference to its diameter is always pi. For 10 points, name this round shape.

clues.t: All the points in a flat plane that are the same distance, the radius, from one center point
Its diameter is a chord through the center, twice as long as the radius and the longest chord of all
Its circumference (distance around) equals π × diameter, or 2πr
Its area equals π times the radius squared (πr²)
A full turn around its center is 360 degrees
A chord joins two points on it; a secant line cuts through it; a tangent line touches it at exactly one point
A tangent line is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, and two tangents from one outside point are equal in length
An arc is a piece of its edge; a sector is a pizza-slice region between two radii
Ones that share a center are concentric; the ring-shaped region between two of them is an annulus
Inscribed angle theorem: an angle formed by two chords meeting on it is half the central angle on the same arc
A cyclic quadrilateral has all four corners on one; its opposite angles add up to 180°
Thales’ theorem: a triangle with one side as a diameter and its third corner on the edge has a right angle
Equation with center (h, k) and radius r: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²
A conic section: a plane slicing a cone at a right angle to its axis; it is an ellipse with eccentricity 0
Has infinitely many lines of symmetry; Venn diagrams show sets as overlapping ones
Ferdinand von Lindemann proved in 1882 that “squaring” it (a square of equal area using compass and straightedge) is impossible
Isoperimetric property: of all closed curves with the same perimeter, it encloses the most area
Descartes’ theorem relates the curvatures (1 ÷ radius) of four that all touch; Frederick Soddy restated it in his 1936 poem “The Kiss Precise”
Book III of Euclid’s _Elements_ is about them; his third postulate says one can be drawn (with a compass) for any center and radius
Apollonius’s problem: draw the ones touching three given ones; points with a fixed distance ratio to two points form one
Ptolemy’s theorem links a cyclic quadrilateral’s diagonals to its sides; when two chords cross, their pieces multiply to equal products
Archimedes: its area equals a right triangle with legs equal to its radius and circumference; legend says he told a Roman soldier not to disturb his drawings of them
Archimedes used 96-sided polygons to show its circumference is between 223/71 and 22/7 times its diameter
One radian cuts off an arc as long as the radius; arc length = radius × angle in radians
On the one with radius 1 centered at the origin, the point at angle θ has coordinates (cos θ, sin θ)
Ptolemy’s model moved planets on small ones called epicycles; Johannes Kepler showed orbits are ellipses instead
Every triangle has exactly one through its three corners, centered at the circumcenter; every regular polygon’s corners lie on one too
Hippocrates of Chios found the exact areas of some crescent-shaped lunes bounded by arcs of two of them

trap.title: Whole shape or one part?
trap.body: Many tossups ask for one part of this shape instead of the whole: the diameter (a chord through the center, twice the radius), the radius, the circumference, a chord, or a tangent line. Others want the number pi, the ratio of the circumference to the diameter, or the sphere, its three-dimensional cousin. Naming the whole shape when the question wants a part loses the tossup.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun in the giveaway. “This shape” means circle; “this segment” or “this length,” with clues like “twice the radius” or “the longest chord,” means diameter; “this number” or “this constant” means pi. A circle is a special ellipse, so “ellipse” only earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: circles (prompt on disks or ellipses; do not accept “diameter” or “sphere”)

topics.name: Factorial
topics.kicker: Multiply every whole number from 1 up to n · Counts the ways to line things up
topics.dates: Exclamation-point notation introduced by Christian Kramp, 1808
topics.briefing: The factorial of a whole number, written with an exclamation point, multiplies it by every smaller whole number down to 1, so 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120. Factorials count the ways to put things in order: three friends can line up in 3! = 6 ways, and a deck of 52 cards can be shuffled into a number of orders with 68 digits. They grow so fast that 70! is bigger than a googol, a 1 followed by 100 zeros.
topics.answerHtml: factorial (accept n factorial or factorial function; do not accept “permutations” or “gamma function”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1808, Christian Kramp introduced the modern symbol for this operation, a punctuation mark written after a number. This operation gives 1 when applied to 0, because multiplying no numbers at all is defined to give 1.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this operation, written with an exclamation point, that multiplies a whole number by every smaller positive whole number.

tossups.p: James Stirling and Abraham de Moivre [“duh MWAHV”] found that, for large n, this function is approximately equal to the square root of 2 pi n, times n over e raised to the nth power. This function grows faster than any exponential function, such as 2 to the n.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this function, written n followed by an exclamation point, that equals 120 when n is 5.

tossups.p: Leonhard Euler extended this function beyond whole numbers with what is now called the gamma function, which makes this function of one-half equal to half the square root of pi. For positive whole numbers n, the gamma function of n equals this function of n minus 1.
tossups.r: This function of n counts the ways to arrange n different objects in a row. For 10 points, name this function, which equals 24 for the number 4.

tossups.p: Wilson’s theorem says that a number p greater than 1 is prime exactly when one more than this function of p minus 1 is divisible by p. This function of 100 ends in exactly 24 zeros, because each zero comes from a 5 paired with a 2.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this function, written with an exclamation point, whose value for 6 is 720.

tossups.p: The number of ways to choose k objects from a group of n equals this function of n divided by the product of this function of k and this function of n minus k. Every entry of Pascal’s triangle can be found with that formula.
tossups.r: This function of 52 counts the orders of a shuffled deck of cards, a number with 68 digits. For 10 points, name this function, which equals 6 for the number 3.

tossups.p: This function of 10 equals 3,628,800, which is exactly the number of seconds in six weeks. Computer programs often compute this function with recursion, multiplying n by the same function of n minus 1.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this function, written with an exclamation point, which multiplies all the whole numbers from 1 up to n.

tossups.p: A traveling salesman who checks every possible route through many cities faces a number of routes that grows like this function of the number of cities. Many calculators show an error for this function of 70, because its value is more than a googol.
tossups.r: Its value for 3 is 6. For 10 points, name this function, which equals 5,040 for the number 7.

tossups.p: Brocard’s [“broh-KARZ”] problem asks when one more than this function of n is a perfect square; the only known examples are n equals 4, 5, and 7. The number 145 equals the sum of this function applied to each of its digits.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this function, written with an exclamation point, whose value at 3 is 6.

tossups.p: If n letters are put into n addressed envelopes so that every letter goes to a wrong address, the number of ways to do it is the whole number closest to this function of n divided by e. Such arrangements, in which nothing lands in its original place, are called derangements.
tossups.r: Eight runners can finish a race in 40,320 different orders, the value of this function at 8. For 10 points, name this function.

tossups.p: In 1677, Fabian Stedman explained how this function counts the different orders in which a set of church bells can be rung, in an English art called change ringing. The only whole numbers equal to this function of themselves are 1 and 2.
tossups.r: Five bells can be rung in 120 different orders, the value of this function at 5. For 10 points, name this function, written with an exclamation point.

tossups.p: The number of positions of a Rubik’s Cube, about 43 quintillion, is found using this function of 8 for the corner pieces and this function of 12 for the edge pieces. This function also fills the denominators of the Taylor series for sine and cosine.
tossups.r: It is written as a number followed by an exclamation point. For 10 points, name this function, which equals 24 for the number 4.

tossups.p: A “double” version of this function multiplies every other whole number, so applied to 7 it gives 7 times 5 times 3 times 1, or 105. The primorial, which multiplies only prime numbers, is named by analogy with this function.
tossups.r: Four different books can be arranged on a shelf in 24 ways, the value of this function at 4. For 10 points, name this function.

tossups.p: Adrien-Marie Legendre’s [“luh-ZHAHN-druhz”] formula finds how many times a prime p divides this function of n by adding up n over p, n over p squared, n over p cubed, and so on, rounding each down.
tossups.r: It counts the 120 ways to arrange the letters of “TOPIC.” For 10 points, name this function, written with an exclamation point.

tossups.p: The number of ways to seat n people around a round table, if rotating everyone counts as the same seating, is this function of n minus 1. Dividing this function of 8 by this function of 5 counts the ways to hand out three different medals among 8 runners.
tossups.r: It is written with an exclamation point. For 10 points, name this function, which equals 6 when applied to 3.

tossups.p: Each term in the infinite series for e to the x is x to the n divided by this function of n, so e itself equals 1 plus 1 plus one-half plus one-sixth, and so on.
tossups.r: Seven people can line up in 5,040 different orders. For 10 points, name this function, written with an exclamation point, that equals 720 for 6.

clues.t: Multiplies a whole number by every smaller positive whole number: n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1
Written with an exclamation point after the number; its value for 5 is 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120
Applied to n, it counts the ways to arrange n different objects in a row (their permutations)
Values to memorize: 3 gives 6, 4 gives 24, 6 gives 720, 7 gives 5,040, and 10 gives 3,628,800
Its value for 0 is 1, because multiplying no numbers at all (the empty product) gives 1
Defined recursively: its value for n is n times its value for n − 1, a classic first example of recursion in programming
Combinations (n choose k) divide its value for n by its values for k and for n − k; they fill Pascal’s triangle
Gold, silver, and bronze medals can go to 3 of 8 runners in 8 × 7 × 6 = 336 ways: its value for 8 divided by its value for 5
A 52-card deck can be shuffled in a number of orders equal to its value for 52, which has 68 digits
Its value for 10, 3,628,800, is exactly the number of seconds in six weeks
Its value for 70 is more than a googol (10^100), so many calculators show an error
Grows faster than any exponential, like 2^n; checking every traveling-salesman route takes time that grows like it
e = 1 + 1 + 1/2 + 1/6 + 1/24 + …, adding 1 over its value for each whole number; it also fills the Taylor series for sine and cosine
n people can sit around a round table in (its value for n − 1) ways, if rotations count as the same seating
Christian Kramp introduced the exclamation-point notation in 1808
Stirling’s approximation (James Stirling and Abraham de Moivre): for large n, it is about √(2πn) × (n/e)^n
Leonhard Euler’s gamma function extends it beyond whole numbers: Γ(n) equals its value for n − 1, and its value for 1/2 is √π ÷ 2
Wilson’s theorem: p > 1 is prime exactly when one more than its value for p − 1 is divisible by p
Its value for 100 ends in exactly 24 zeros, one for each factor of 5 paired with a factor of 2
Legendre’s formula: the power of a prime p in its value for n is n/p + n/p² + n/p³ + …, each rounded down
Brocard’s problem: one more than its value for n is a perfect square for n = 4, 5, and 7, the only known cases
145 is the sum of its values for 1, 4, and 5; only 1, 2, 145, and 40,585 equal the sum of its values for their digits
Derangements (nothing left in its original place): the count is the whole number nearest its value for n, divided by e
The double version multiplies every other number, so for 7 it gives 7 × 5 × 3 × 1 = 105
The primorial, which multiplies only prime numbers, is named by analogy with it
In 1677, Fabian Stedman used it to count the orders for ringing church bells (change ringing)
The Rubik’s Cube’s 43 quintillion positions are counted using its values for 8 (corner pieces) and 12 (edge pieces)
The only whole numbers equal to their own value of it are 1 and 2

trap.title: Function or arrangements?
trap.body: Factorials count permutations, so a tossup about lining things up may want “permutations,” and one about choosing groups may want “combinations” or “binomial coefficients.” The gamma function extends the factorial to fractions, but it is its own answer line. Don’t mix factorials up with exponents either: 5! means 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1, not 5 × 5 × 5 × 5 × 5.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This function” or “this operation,” written with an exclamation point, means factorial. “These arrangements” or “these orderings” means permutations, and a function named for a Greek letter that also works for fractions means the gamma function.
trap.line: Real answer line: factorial (accept n factorial; do not accept “permutations” or “gamma function”)

topics.name: Pi
topics.kicker: Circumference ÷ diameter ≈ 3.14159 · Its digits never end or repeat
topics.dates: Symbol π first used by William Jones, 1706
topics.briefing: Pi (π) is the number you get when you divide any circle’s circumference by its diameter: about 3.14159, no matter how big or small the circle is. Its digits go on forever without repeating, and computers have calculated trillions of them, while people around the world celebrate Pi Day every March 14. The ancient Greek mathematician Archimedes was one of the first to pin it down, proving it is a little less than 22/7.
topics.answerHtml: pi (or π; accept Archimedes’ constant or Ludolph’s number; prompt on 3.14 or other decimal approximations)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1882, Ferdinand von Lindemann proved that this number is transcendental, meaning it is not a root of any polynomial with whole-number coefficients. His proof showed that squaring the circle with only a compass and straightedge is impossible.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this constant, about 3.14159, the ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter.

tossups.p: Johann Heinrich Lambert proved in 1761 that this number cannot be written as a fraction of two whole numbers. A run of six 9s in a row begins at the 762nd decimal place of this number, a spot named for physicist Richard Feynman.
tossups.r: The fraction 22 over 7 is a common estimate of it. For 10 points, name this number, about 3.14.

tossups.p: William Jones first used a Greek letter as the symbol for this number in 1706, and Leonhard Euler made that symbol popular. In Euler’s identity, e raised to the power of i times this number, plus 1, equals 0.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mathematical constant, which equals a circle’s circumference divided by its diameter.

tossups.p: Archimedes trapped this number between 223 over 71 and 22 over 7 by drawing polygons with 96 sides inside and outside a circle. Because of that work, this number is sometimes named after Archimedes.
tossups.r: Its decimal expansion begins 3.14159. For 10 points, name this number that you multiply by a circle’s diameter to get its circumference.

tossups.p: In the 400s CE, the Chinese mathematician Zu Chongzhi [“zoo chong-JUR”] found the fraction 355 over 113 for this number, which is correct to six decimal places. The Rhind Papyrus from ancient Egypt implies a value of about 3.16 for it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this constant, roughly 3.14, the ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter.

tossups.p: Ludolph van Ceulen [“LOO-dolf vahn KUH-len”] spent years computing 35 decimal places of this number, and the digits were carved on his tombstone. In 1873, William Shanks published 707 decimal places of it, but he had made a mistake at the 528th decimal place.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, whose decimal digits begin 3.14159 and never end.

tossups.p: In 1897, the Indiana House of Representatives passed a bill, written by an amateur mathematician, that would have given this number an incorrect value, but the state Senate set it aside after a Purdue professor pointed out the error.
tossups.r: A full turn of 360 degrees equals two times this number in radians. For 10 points, name this constant, about 3.14.

tossups.p: Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon [“boo-FOHN”], worked out the chance that a needle dropped onto a floor marked with evenly spaced lines lands across a line, a problem later used to estimate this number. That chance has this number in its denominator.
tossups.r: It is the ratio of any circle’s circumference to its diameter. For 10 points, name this number, about 3.14.

tossups.p: Madhava [“MAH-duh-vuh”] of Sangamagrama and, much later, Gottfried Leibniz found that 1 minus one-third plus one-fifth minus one-seventh, and so on forever, equals this number divided by 4. Leonhard Euler showed that adding up the reciprocals of all the perfect squares gives this number squared, divided by 6.
tossups.r: Multiplying it by a circle’s diameter gives the circumference. For 10 points, name this constant, roughly 3.14159.

tossups.p: In 1914, Srinivasa Ramanujan [“rah-MAH-nuh-jun”] published infinite series that close in on 1 divided by this number very quickly. In 2019, Emma Haruka Iwao [“ee-WAH-oh”] used cloud computers to set a record by calculating more than 31 trillion digits of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, which you multiply by the radius squared to find a circle’s area.

tossups.p: The Bible’s First Book of Kings describes a round bronze basin 10 cubits across and 30 cubits around, which suggests a value of 3 for this number. A Babylonian clay tablet implies a value of 3 and one-eighth for it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, which is the ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter.

tossups.p: The narrator of a 2001 novel by Yann Martel, who survives at sea in a lifeboat with a Bengal tiger, shortens his first name to match this number. Many people memorize this number with the sentence “May I have a large container of coffee,” whose word lengths give its first eight digits.
tossups.r: Its symbol is the 16th letter of the Greek alphabet. For 10 points, name this number, about 3.14.

tossups.p: John Wallis wrote half of this number as an endless product of fractions: 2 over 1, times 2 over 3, times 4 over 3, times 4 over 5, and so on. François Viète [“frahn-SWAH vee-ET”] found an earlier endless product for this number built from nested square roots of 2.
tossups.r: It is about 3.14. For 10 points, name this number, which gives a circle’s circumference when multiplied by its diameter.

tossups.p: The total area under the bell-shaped curve of e to the negative x squared is the square root of this number. That is why the formula for the normal distribution in statistics includes the square root of 2 times this number.
tossups.r: A sphere’s volume is four-thirds times this number times the radius cubed. For 10 points, name this constant, about 3.14.

tossups.p: Larry Shaw started a holiday for this number at San Francisco’s Exploratorium science museum in 1988, and the U.S. House of Representatives officially recognized that holiday in 2009. The holiday falls on Albert Einstein’s birthday.
tossups.r: That holiday is March 14, or 3/14. For 10 points, name this number, the ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter.

clues.t: The ratio of any circle’s circumference to its diameter; it is the same for every circle
About 3.14159; common approximations are 3.14 and 22/7
In the circle formulas: circumference = it × diameter, and area = it × radius squared
Written with a Greek letter, the 16th letter of the Greek alphabet
Celebrated every March 14 (3/14), which is also Albert Einstein’s birthday
Irrational: its decimal digits never end and never repeat (proved by Johann Heinrich Lambert in 1761)
Archimedes used 96-sided polygons to trap it between 223/71 and 22/7, so it is sometimes named for him
Euler’s identity: e to the power of i times it, plus 1, equals 0
A full turn of 360° equals 2 times it in radians, so 180° equals it in radians
A sphere’s volume is 4/3 × it × r³, and a sphere’s surface area is 4 × it × r²
Tau, written τ, equals twice it; some mathematicians argue that tau is the better circle constant
Mnemonic: “May I have a large container of coffee” has word lengths 3-1-4-1-5-9-2-6
The narrator of Yann Martel’s 2001 novel, stranded on a lifeboat with a Bengal tiger, takes his nickname from it
William Jones first used the Greek letter for it in 1706; Leonhard Euler made the symbol popular
Ferdinand von Lindemann proved it transcendental in 1882, so squaring the circle with compass and straightedge is impossible
The Feynman point: six 9s in a row starting at the 762nd decimal place
Ludolph van Ceulen’s 35 decimal places were carved on his tombstone; only the first 527 of William Shanks’s 707 decimal places (1873) were right
Zu Chongzhi’s fraction 355/113 (5th century CE, China) is correct to six decimal places
The Bible’s First Book of Kings implies 3; a Babylonian tablet implies 3 1/8; Egypt’s Rhind Papyrus implies about 3.16
Madhava, and much later Leibniz: 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − 1/7 + … equals one-fourth of it
Basel problem: Euler showed that 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + … equals its square divided by 6
Endless products: John Wallis’s 2/1 × 2/3 × 4/3 × 4/5 × … equals half of it; François Viète used nested square roots of 2
Buffon’s needle: dropping needles onto evenly spaced lines can be used to estimate it
In 1897, the Indiana House passed a bill that would have given it a wrong value; the state Senate set the bill aside
Ramanujan’s 1914 series close in on 1 over it very quickly; Emma Haruka Iwao computed over 31 trillion digits in 2019
The bell curve e^(−x²) has a total area equal to its square root, so the normal distribution formula contains it
Larry Shaw started its holiday at San Francisco’s Exploratorium in 1988; the U.S. House recognized the holiday in 2009

trap.title: Which famous constant?
trap.body: Several constants share the same kinds of clues. The number e (about 2.718) is the base of natural logarithms and also appears in Euler’s identity; the golden ratio, phi (about 1.618), is linked to the Fibonacci sequence; and tau equals 2 times pi. Buzzing on “Euler” or “infinite series” alone can land you on the wrong one.
trap.fix: Listen for circles: circumference, diameter, area, radians, or 3.14 mean pi. Compound interest, natural logarithms, or 2.718 mean e; pentagons, Fibonacci numbers, or 1.618 mean the golden ratio. Saying only “3.14” earns a prompt, so name the constant.
trap.line: Real answer line: pi (or π; accept Archimedes’ constant; prompt on 3.14)

topics.name: Pythagorean theorem
topics.kicker: In a right triangle, a² + b² = c² · Named for Pythagoras of Samos
topics.briefing: The Pythagorean theorem says that in any right triangle, the squares of the two shorter sides add up to the square of the longest side, the hypotenuse: a² + b² = c². A triangle with sides 3, 4, and 5 fits the rule, since 9 + 16 = 25. The rule is named for the Greek thinker Pythagoras, but Babylonian scribes were using it more than 1,000 years before he lived, and people have since found hundreds of different proofs.
topics.answerHtml: Pythagorean theorem (or Pythagoras’s theorem; accept a² + b² = c²; prompt on Pythagoras)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Elisha Scott Loomis collected more than 300 different proofs of this theorem in one book. In 1876, five years before becoming president, Congressman James Garfield published a new proof of it using a trapezoid split into three right triangles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theorem, which states that a squared plus b squared equals c squared in a right triangle.

tossups.p: Proposition 47 in Book I of Euclid’s _Elements_ proves this theorem with a diagram nicknamed the “bride’s chair.” The very next proposition proves its converse: if the squares on two sides of a triangle add up to the square on the third side, the triangle has a right angle.
tossups.r: It is usually written a squared plus b squared equals c squared. For 10 points, name this theorem about right triangles.

tossups.p: The Babylonian clay tablet Plimpton 322, made around 1800 BCE, lists numbers linked to whole-number solutions of this theorem’s equation. Such solutions include 5, 12, and 13, as well as 8, 15, and 17.
tossups.r: The simplest such set is 3, 4, and 5. For 10 points, name this theorem about the sides of right triangles.

tossups.p: Chinese mathematicians named this theorem with the words gou and gu for a right triangle’s short and long legs, and the ancient Chinese text _Zhoubi Suanjing_ [“JOH-bee swahn-JING”] discusses it for sides of 3, 4, and 5. An Indian text called the Baudhayana [“bow-DHAH-yuh-nuh”] Shulba Sutra states it for the diagonal of a rectangle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theorem stating that the squares of a right triangle’s legs add up to the square of its hypotenuse.

tossups.p: Pierre de Fermat claimed that this theorem’s equation has no solutions in positive whole numbers once its exponent of 2 is replaced by any larger whole number, a claim Andrew Wiles finally proved in the 1990s. Whole-number solutions do exist for the original equation, such as 7, 24, and 25.
tossups.r: Its equation relates the legs and the hypotenuse of a right triangle. For 10 points, name this theorem that says a squared plus b squared equals c squared.

tossups.p: The law of cosines generalizes this theorem by subtracting 2 times a times b times the cosine of the angle between sides a and b. When that angle is 90 degrees, its cosine is zero, and the law of cosines becomes this theorem.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theorem used to find a missing side of a right triangle.

tossups.p: A baseball formula by Bill James that squares a team’s runs scored and runs allowed is nicknamed for this theorem. In the 1939 film _The Wizard of Oz_, the Scarecrow recites a garbled version of this theorem after receiving a diploma, wrongly mentioning square roots and an isosceles triangle.
tossups.r: This theorem says the hypotenuse squared equals the sum of the squares of the legs. For 10 points, name this theorem about right triangles.

tossups.p: The diagonal between opposite corners of a box with side lengths a, b, and c has length equal to the square root of a squared plus b squared plus c squared, which comes from using this theorem twice. On a coordinate grid, the distance formula comes directly from this theorem.
tossups.r: It applies only to triangles with a 90-degree angle. For 10 points, name this theorem used to find the hypotenuse of a right triangle.

tossups.p: Applying this theorem to a point on a circle of radius 1 gives the identity that sine squared plus cosine squared equals 1 for every angle. This theorem shows that a square with sides of length 1 has a diagonal whose length is the square root of 2.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theorem, which says that the two legs of a right triangle, squared and added, equal the hypotenuse squared.

tossups.p: The 12th-century Indian mathematician Bhaskara [“BAHS-kuh-ruh”] is said to have proved this theorem with a single diagram labeled only “Behold!” One common proof of it places four copies of a right triangle inside a large square and compares the uncovered areas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theorem, which says a squared plus b squared equals c squared for any right triangle.

tossups.p: De Gua’s theorem extends this theorem to a triangular pyramid with three right angles at one corner, using the areas of its faces. Builders use the converse of this theorem to check square corners by measuring 6, 8, and 10 units.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theorem about the legs and the hypotenuse of a right triangle.

tossups.p: Followers of this theorem’s namesake are said to have used it to discover that the diagonal of a square with side 1 cannot be written as a fraction. This theorem is named for a Greek thinker from Samos who founded a brotherhood in Croton [“KROH-tun”], in southern Italy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theorem stating that, in a right triangle, the squares of the legs add up to the square of the hypotenuse.

tossups.p: Euclid gave a formula that builds whole-number solutions to this theorem’s equation from two numbers m and n, using m squared minus n squared, 2 m n, and m squared plus n squared. In every such solution, at least one of the three numbers is a multiple of 5.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theorem, written a squared plus b squared equals c squared, about right triangles.

tossups.p: Combined with the fact that a 30-60-90 triangle is half of an equilateral triangle, this theorem shows that the longer leg of that triangle is the square root of 3 times the shorter leg. It also explains why the hypotenuse of a 45-45-90 triangle is the square root of 2 times either leg.
tossups.r: It works only for right triangles. For 10 points, name this theorem that relates the three sides of any right triangle.

tossups.p: Applying Ptolemy’s theorem to a rectangle, whose two diagonals are equal, immediately gives this theorem. A television sold as a 50-inch model is measured along its diagonal, which can be found from the screen’s width and height using this theorem.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theorem about the lengths of the three sides of a right triangle.

trap.title: Theorem, triple, or person?
trap.body: Some tossups want the whole-number solutions themselves, Pythagorean triples like 3-4-5, and others want the man Pythagoras or his followers, the Pythagoreans. Tossups on the law of cosines or the distance formula use this theorem as a clue but want a different answer. Fermat’s Last Theorem looks like this theorem with bigger exponents, but it is its own answer line.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this theorem” or “this equation” means the Pythagorean theorem; “these sets of numbers” means Pythagorean triples; “this man” or “this philosopher” means Pythagoras. Saying only “Pythagoras” on a theorem tossup earns a prompt, so add “theorem.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Pythagorean theorem (or Pythagoras’s theorem; accept a² + b² = c²; prompt on Pythagoras)

topics.name: Matrices
topics.kicker: Rectangular grids of numbers · The workhorses of linear algebra
topics.briefing: A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers arranged in rows and columns, a bit like a tiny spreadsheet. Matrices let mathematicians solve many equations at once, rotate and stretch shapes in computer graphics, and describe how particles behave in quantum physics. Matrices of the same size add entry by entry, but multiplying them follows a row-times-column rule, and switching the order often changes the answer.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: James Joseph Sylvester named these objects in 1850 after the Latin word for “womb,” and Arthur Cayley described their algebra in an 1858 memoir. The Cayley–Hamilton theorem says that every square one of these satisfies its own characteristic equation.
tossups.r: They can be added only when they are the same size. For 10 points, name these rectangular arrays of numbers arranged in rows and columns.

tossups.p: In 1925, Max Born realized that the tables of numbers in Werner Heisenberg’s new form of quantum mechanics followed the multiplication rule for these objects. The three Pauli examples of these objects are 2-by-2 arrays used to describe the spin of an electron.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rectangular grids of numbers, which are multiplied by combining rows with columns.

tossups.p: The ancient Chinese book _The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art_ solved systems of equations by arranging their coefficients in grids of counting rods, an early use of these objects. Gaussian elimination solves such systems by reducing one of these objects to row echelon form.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these arrays of numbers with rows and columns, studied in linear algebra.

tossups.p: Multiplying two of these objects in the opposite order often gives a different result, so their multiplication is not commutative. Two of these objects can be multiplied only if the first one has as many columns as the second one has rows.
tossups.r: An m-by-n one of these has m rows and n columns. For 10 points, name these rectangular arrays of numbers.

tossups.p: A square one of these objects has an inverse exactly when its determinant is not zero; if the determinant is zero, it is called singular. Multiplying any square one of these by the identity one, which has 1s along its main diagonal and 0s everywhere else, leaves it unchanged.
tossups.r: They are written inside large brackets. For 10 points, name these arrays of numbers, such as a 2-by-2 grid.

tossups.p: For an orthogonal one of these objects, the transpose is also the inverse. The transpose of one of these flips it across its main diagonal, turning its rows into columns, and a symmetric one is equal to its own transpose.
tossups.r: Each number inside one is called an entry. For 10 points, name these rectangular arrays of numbers used in linear algebra.

tossups.p: The trace of one of these objects is the sum of the numbers on its main diagonal, which also equals the sum of its eigenvalues. One of these objects acts on each of its eigenvectors by simply scaling it along the same line.
tossups.r: A square one has as many rows as columns. For 10 points, name these grids of numbers, which have rows and columns.

tossups.p: To invert a 2-by-2 one of these objects, swap the two entries on its main diagonal, change the signs of the other two entries, and divide everything by the determinant. Computer graphics cards are designed to multiply these objects quickly.
tossups.r: One with a single row is called a row vector. For 10 points, name these rectangular arrays of numbers.

tossups.p: Rotating every point of a plane around the origin by an angle theta can be done by multiplying by one of these objects whose top row is cosine theta, negative sine theta. In 3D computer graphics, 4-by-4 ones of these objects are used to move, turn, and resize models.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these grids of numbers, which have rows and columns and are studied in linear algebra.

tossups.p: Google’s original PageRank method ranked web pages by finding an eigenvector of a giant one of these objects built from the links between pages. In a Markov chain, the probabilities of moving between states are stored in a “transition” one of these objects.
tossups.r: Their sum is found by adding matching entries. For 10 points, name these rectangular arrays of numbers, studied in linear algebra.

tossups.p: Wassily Leontief [“vah-SEE-lee lee-ON-tee-ef”] won the 1973 Nobel Prize in economics for input–output models that use these objects to show how industries depend on one another. The adjacency one of these objects for a graph records which pairs of points are connected.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rectangular grids of numbers, which can be added, subtracted, and multiplied.

tossups.p: In multivariable calculus, the Hessian is one of these objects made of second partial derivatives, while the Jacobian is one made of first partial derivatives. A sparse one of these objects has mostly zeros as its entries.
tossups.r: A diagonal one has zeros everywhere except its main diagonal. For 10 points, name these rectangular arrays of numbers.

tossups.p: The rank of one of these objects is the number of linearly independent rows it has, which always equals its number of linearly independent columns. Gauss–Jordan elimination puts one of these objects into reduced row echelon form.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rectangular arrays of numbers, which can represent systems of linear equations.

tossups.p: The singular value decomposition breaks any one of these objects into a product of three special ones, including a diagonal one. The LU decomposition writes many square ones of these as a lower triangular one times an upper triangular one.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rectangular arrays of numbers, which are multiplied row by column.

tossups.p: A Hermitian [“her-MISH-un”] one of these objects equals its own conjugate transpose, and all of its eigenvalues are real numbers. In quantum mechanics, measurable quantities like energy are represented by Hermitian ones of these objects.
tossups.r: One with a single column is called a column vector. For 10 points, name these rectangular arrays of numbers.

clues.t: A rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns
Described by size: an m × n one has m rows and n columns; a square one has equally many of each
The main tool of linear algebra, used to solve systems of linear equations
Each number inside is an entry; two of the same size are added entry by entry
Multiplied row by column: the first one needs as many columns as the second one has rows
Their multiplication is not commutative: AB often does not equal BA
The identity one has 1s on the main diagonal and 0s elsewhere; multiplying by it changes nothing
A square one has an inverse only when its determinant is not zero; otherwise it is called singular
The transpose flips rows into columns; a symmetric one equals its transpose, and an orthogonal one’s transpose is its inverse
Each eigenvector is simply scaled by it along the same line; the scale factors are its eigenvalues
The trace is the sum of the main-diagonal entries, which also equals the sum of the eigenvalues
Gaussian elimination row-reduces one to row echelon form; Gauss–Jordan elimination goes on to reduced row echelon form
Computer graphics use them to rotate, move, and resize images; graphics cards are built to multiply them fast
One with a single row is a row vector; one with a single column is a column vector
James Joseph Sylvester named them in 1850, from the Latin word for “womb”
Arthur Cayley’s 1858 memoir set out their algebra; Cayley–Hamilton theorem: each square one satisfies its own characteristic equation
China’s _The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art_ solved equations by laying out coefficients in counting-rod grids
Max Born realized in 1925 that Werner Heisenberg’s quantum mechanics followed their multiplication rule
The three Pauli ones are 2 × 2 arrays that describe the spin of an electron
A Hermitian one equals its conjugate transpose and has only real eigenvalues; such ones represent measurable quantities in quantum mechanics
The 2 × 2 one that rotates the plane by θ has top row (cos θ, −sin θ); 3D graphics use 4 × 4 ones
To invert a 2 × 2 one, swap the two main-diagonal entries, change the signs of the other two, and divide by the determinant
Google’s PageRank found an eigenvector of a giant one built from web links; a Markov chain keeps its probabilities in a transition one
Wassily Leontief won the 1973 economics Nobel for input–output models built from them
A graph’s adjacency one records which pairs of points are connected
The Hessian holds second partial derivatives and the Jacobian holds first partial derivatives; a sparse one is mostly zeros
Rank: the number of linearly independent rows, which always equals the number of linearly independent columns

trap.title: The array, not its number
trap.body: Many clues about matrices really describe a single number computed from one, the determinant (ad − bc for a 2 × 2), and a tossup asking for “this quantity” or “this value” wants determinant, not matrix. Eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and vectors are also separate answer lines that share many of the same clues.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “These arrays” or “these objects with rows and columns” means matrices; “this scalar,” “this value,” or “ad minus bc” means the determinant; “these special numbers λ” means eigenvalues. Saying “array” earns a prompt, so be ready to say “matrix.”
trap.line: Real answer line: matrices (or matrix; prompt on arrays; do not accept “determinant”)

topics.name: Determinant
topics.kicker: One number computed from a square matrix · Zero means no inverse
topics.briefing: The determinant is a single number calculated from a square matrix. For a 2 × 2 matrix with rows a, b and c, d, it equals ad − bc, and it tells you how much the matrix stretches or shrinks areas. If the determinant is zero, the matrix squashes space flat and has no inverse, which is why mathematicians check it before solving systems of equations.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Seki Takakazu [“SEH-kee tah-kah-KAH-zoo”] in Japan and Gottfried Leibniz in Germany each discovered this quantity in the late 1600s while studying systems of equations. This quantity for a product of two square matrices equals the product of their separate values of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number computed from a square matrix, which equals ad minus bc for a 2-by-2 matrix.

tossups.p: Cramer’s rule solves a system of linear equations by dividing two values of this quantity, one of them found after replacing a column of the coefficient matrix with the constants from the right side of the equations. Gabriel Cramer published that rule in 1750.
tossups.r: If this quantity is zero, the matrix has no inverse. For 10 points, name this number calculated from a square matrix.

tossups.p: For a 3-by-3 matrix whose rows are three vectors, the absolute value of this quantity is the volume of the parallelepiped [“pair-uh-lel-uh-PIE-ped”] they form; for two vectors in a plane, its absolute value is the area of their parallelogram. A negative value of this quantity means a transformation flips space like a mirror.
tossups.r: It equals ad minus bc for a 2-by-2 matrix. For 10 points, name this number, which is zero for any square matrix with no inverse.

tossups.p: Setting this quantity for A minus lambda times the identity matrix equal to zero gives the characteristic equation, whose solutions are the eigenvalues of A. This quantity for any square matrix equals the product of all its eigenvalues.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, written with vertical bars around a matrix, that equals ad minus bc for a 2-by-2 matrix.

tossups.p: The cross product of two vectors can be found by computing this quantity for a 3-by-3 array whose top row holds the unit vectors i, j, and k. The rule of Sarrus [“sah-ROOS”] is a shortcut for finding this quantity for a 3-by-3 matrix by multiplying along its diagonals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number computed from a square matrix, which is zero when the matrix cannot be inverted.

tossups.p: Swapping two rows of a matrix flips the sign of this quantity, while adding a multiple of one row to another row leaves it unchanged. This quantity for a triangular matrix is simply the product of the entries on its main diagonal.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, which equals ad minus bc for the 2-by-2 matrix with rows a, b and c, d.

tossups.p: Laplace expansion finds this quantity by working along any one row or column and combining it with values of this quantity for smaller square pieces, called minors. The Leibniz formula writes this quantity as a sum over all permutations, so a 4-by-4 matrix needs 24 terms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this value calculated from a square matrix, which tells whether the matrix has an inverse.

tossups.p: The Wronskian [“RON-skee-un”] is a version of this quantity used to test whether solutions of a differential equation are linearly independent. The Jacobian version of this quantity tells how much a change of variables stretches area in a double integral.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number computed from a square matrix, which is zero exactly when the matrix has no inverse.

tossups.p: Alexandre-Théophile Vandermonde [“vahn-dair-MOHND”] names a special matrix whose value of this quantity equals the product of all the differences between its variables. Arthur Cayley introduced the notation of vertical bars around a grid of numbers for this quantity in 1841.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, found for a 2-by-2 matrix by computing ad minus bc.

tossups.p: Every rotation matrix has this quantity equal to exactly 1, while every reflection matrix has it equal to negative 1. A square matrix is called singular when this quantity equals 0.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number calculated from a square matrix, such as ad minus bc for a 2-by-2 one.

tossups.p: Carl Friedrich Gauss used this quantity’s name in 1801 for a number linked to quadratic forms, and Augustin-Louis Cauchy gave the name its modern meaning in 1812. James Joseph Sylvester named matrices because he saw them as grids out of which values of this quantity can be formed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number computed from a square matrix, which is not zero exactly when the matrix has an inverse.

tossups.p: This quantity is the same for a matrix and for its transpose, and this quantity for a matrix’s inverse is the reciprocal of its value for the matrix. Multiplying every entry of a 3-by-3 matrix by 2 multiplies this quantity by 8.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, which equals ad minus bc for a 2-by-2 matrix.

tossups.p: Half of the absolute value of this quantity, computed from the coordinates of three points, gives the area of the triangle they form, an idea behind the shoelace formula. If this quantity is zero, the three points lie on one straight line.
tossups.r: It tells whether a square matrix has an inverse. For 10 points, name this number, which equals ad minus bc for a 2-by-2 matrix.

tossups.p: Charles Dodgson, better known as the author of _Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland_, invented a “condensation” method for computing this quantity. For the matrix with rows 3, 1 and 4, 2, this quantity equals 2.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number found from a square matrix, which must be nonzero for the matrix to have an inverse.

tossups.p: The permanent of a matrix is calculated just like this quantity, except that all of its terms are added and none are subtracted. This quantity equals 1 for the identity matrix and 0 for any square matrix with two identical rows.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, calculated as ad minus bc for a 2-by-2 matrix, which shows whether a matrix can be inverted.

For a 2 × 2 matrix with rows a, b and c, d, it equals ad − bc
A square matrix has an inverse exactly when this number is not zero

If it is zero, the matrix is called singular and cannot be inverted
Its absolute value gives the area of a parallelogram (from two vectors) or the volume of a parallelepiped (from three)
A negative value means the transformation flips orientation, like a mirror
Multiplicative: its value for a product AB equals its value for A times its value for B
Cramer’s rule (Gabriel Cramer, 1750) solves linear systems using ratios of these numbers
Equals the product of the eigenvalues; setting its value for A − λI equal to zero gives the characteristic equation
Swapping two rows flips its sign; adding a multiple of one row to another leaves it unchanged
For a triangular matrix it is the product of the main-diagonal entries; for the identity matrix it is 1
The cross product of two vectors can be found as one of these with i, j, and k in the top row
It is 0 for any square matrix with two identical rows or with a row of all zeros
Discovered independently by Seki Takakazu in Japan (1683) and by Gottfried Leibniz (1693)
Gauss used its name in 1801 for quadratic forms; Augustin-Louis Cauchy gave the name its modern meaning in 1812
Arthur Cayley introduced its vertical-bar notation (1841); James Joseph Sylvester named matrices (1850) as the “womb” these numbers come from
The rule of Sarrus finds the 3 × 3 value by multiplying along diagonals
Laplace (cofactor) expansion works along any row or column, using smaller ones called minors and cofactors
The Leibniz formula sums over all permutations, so a 4 × 4 matrix needs 24 terms
The Wronskian, one of these built from functions, tests whether solutions of a differential equation are linearly independent
The Jacobian one measures how a change of variables stretches area in a double integral
The Vandermonde one equals the product of all the differences between its variables
Rotation matrices have it equal to 1; reflection matrices have it equal to −1
It is the same for a matrix and its transpose; the inverse has the reciprocal value; doubling every entry of an n × n matrix multiplies it by 2^n
Half its absolute value, from three points’ coordinates, is their triangle’s area (the shoelace idea); zero means the points are collinear
Charles Dodgson (Lewis Carroll) invented a “condensation” method for computing it

trap.title: Number, not the matrix
trap.body: Clues about matrices and determinants overlap, but a determinant is a single number while a matrix is the whole rectangular array. Tossups that ask for “these arrays” want matrices, and ones that ask for the special values λ want eigenvalues. Don’t confuse it with the discriminant, b² − 4ac, either: that number tells how many real roots a quadratic has.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this quantity,” “this value,” or “this scalar,” plus “ad − bc” or “zero means no inverse,” means determinant. “These arrays,” “rows and columns,” or “multiplied row by column” means matrices.
trap.line: Real answer line: determinant (accept det; do not accept “matrix”)
